extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, economists, and researchers studying patent litigation and patent value
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis identifying and comparing characteristics of the most-litigated U.S. patents versus patents litigated only once, using counts, citation metrics, technology/industry classifications, owner characteristics, and regression analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of nonprovisional U.S. applications in chain (use of continuations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of nonprovisional U.S. applications (original plus continuations/divisionals) leading to the patent. The most-litigated patents averaged 4.32 applications vs. 2.0 in the control set; median most-litigated = 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High use of continuations is a distinguishing characteristic of most-litigated patents and may reflect applicants 'bulletproofing' patents they expect to litigate. See citation to Lemley & Moore on continuations. Treat continuation counts as an indicator but consider why applicants file continuations (strategy, uncertainty, drafting style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Total number of forward citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw count of citations received by subsequent patents referring back to the patent in question (used as a common measure of patent value). The most-litigated patents have markedly higher forward citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward citations are often used as evidence of patent value, but raw counts can be misleading because older patents have more time to accumulate citations. Use with age-adjustment and log-transformation due to skew. See Hall, Jaffe & Trajtenberg and other empirical literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusted number of forward citations (cohort normalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forward citations normalized by patent 'cohort' (patents issued the same year). For each patent, divide its forward citations by the cohort average; then average those adjusted values across the data set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cohort adjustment corrects for age effects and changing citation patterns over time. The paper uses one-year cohorts (method from Hall et al.). After adjustment and log-transformation, differences between most-litigated and control patents are highly significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of self-citations (and adjusted self-citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of forward citations where the citing patent is from the same owner/assignee or (by the authors' decision rule) where inventors are identical and there are no co-inventors; treated as a subset of forward citations and an independent indicator of private value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-citations indicate portfolio-building and private value beyond overall forward citations. The authors use a detailed decision rule (owner same OR owners different but inventors same and no co-inventors) and manually examined front pages of forward-citing patents to identify self-citations. Note difficulties in identification when ownership changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Total number of claims in the patent document. Most-litigated patents averaged ~39.3 claims vs ~24.5 in once-litigated patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number of claims is sometimes associated with patent value but the relationship is complex: claim count can reflect drafting style, resource constraints, uncertainty, or perceived importance rather than intrinsic breadth. Use cautiously and consider complementary indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of references to prior U.S. patents (backward citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of prior U.S. patents cited in prosecution (examiner- or applicant-cited). Most-litigated patents cite substantially more U.S. patents than once-litigated patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More prior patent references may signal stronger examination and fewer uncited invalidating references—potentially greater validity and value. May also reflect applicant efforts to 'bulletproof' patents expected to be litigated. Use in conjunction with other measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of references to foreign patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of cited foreign patents in the prior art references list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as part of backward-citation profile; most-litigated patents show higher counts. Interpret together with U.S. patent references and nonpatent literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of nonpatent references (printed publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of nonpatent prior art references (printed publications) cited during prosecution. Most-litigated patents cite many more nonpatent references (nearly ten times) than once-litigated patents on average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonpatent references are a strong distinguishing feature. Because most nonpatent prior art is supplied by applicants rather than examiners, high counts likely reflect applicant-provided 'bulletproofing'. Treat as an indicator of applicant effort and perceived value; adjust for PTO practice changes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Log-transformation for skewed metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply log transformation to skewed variables (e.g., forward citations) to make distributions more comparable and highlight differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because forward citations and similar measures are highly skewed, report both raw and log-transformed statistics; statistical tests (one-sample t-tests) are performed on log-transformed values where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bivariate comparison using one-sample t-test (with log transformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare proportions or means between most-litigated and once-litigated sets using bivariate t-tests on log-transformed variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout to test significance of differences in means/proportions. Report p-values and indicate whether differences are significant (e.g., p < 0.0001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-area classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize patents by technology area (e.g., software total, pure software, software-business-method, mechanical, electronics, imaging, biotechnology, chemistry). The most-litigated set is heavily weighted toward software and imaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents may belong to more than one technology area (non-mutually exclusive). Compare proportions in each area between datasets; report p-values for differences. Recognize overlap between technology and industry classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-area classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize patents by industry (e.g., computer, semiconductors, electronics, medical, pharmaceutical, biotechnology, chemical, communications, transportation, energy and utilities, financial, consumer goods and services, construction). The most-litigated patents are disproportionately in computer and communications industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with technology areas, patents can be associated with multiple industries. Report proportions and statistical significance of differences between datasets. Use industry-area logistic regressions to test predictive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entity size and assignment status (small vs large; assigned before litigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify patent owner size at issue (small vs large entity) and whether the patent was assigned to another owner before litigation. Many patents are sold before litigation; assignment is more common among most-litigated patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment before litigation correlates with increased litigation likelihood; small-entity counts can be skewed by dominant owners (e.g., Katz), so authors excluded Katz patents from small-entity analysis. Consider owners at issuance vs owner at time of suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entity-status taxonomy (12 classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify plaintiff/owner into 12 entity classes: (1) Acquired patents; (2) University heritage or tie; (3) Failed startup; (4) Corporate heritage; (5) Individual-inventor-started company; (6) University/Government/NGO; (7) Startup, pre-product; (8) Product company; (9) Individual; (10) Undetermined; (11) Industry consortium; (12) IP subsidiary of product company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the taxonomy to distinguish practicing companies from nonpracticing entities (NPEs) and inventor-owned licensing entities. Report counts and percentages by class and test differences between most-litigated and once-litigated sets. Weighting by number of suits can change the interpretation (e.g., >80% of suits on most-litigated patents filed by NPEs after weighting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of lawsuits per patent (litigation frequency) and weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of lawsuits filed on each patent; some patents are litigated many times (range observed up to 97 suits). Use counts to weight analyses of entity classes and to interpret impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighting entity-status by number of suits reveals that a small number of patents (and owners) produce a disproportionate number of suits. Report totals (e.g., 2987 suits on 106 most-litigated patents) and recalculate shares when weighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Katz effect (outlier owner influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize outsized influence by a single patent owner (Ronald S. Katz) who owned many top most-litigated patents—Katz-related lawsuits accounted for ~60% (1789 of 2987) of patent-lawsuit combinations in the most-litigated set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to exclude such dominant actors in robustness checks. Authors considered removing Katz but kept him, arguing that outliers are part of the patent system and should be included in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistic regression predictor variables (significant continuous covariates)
rubrics_metrics.description: In multivariate logistic regressions predicting membership in the most-litigated set, three continuous variables were consistently significant: (1) number of U.S. nonprovisional applications leading to the patent; (2) number of references to prior U.S. patents; (3) number of references to nonpatent prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report p-values for technology- and industry-area regressions (e.g., technology: number of apps p = 0.0303; prior U.S. references p = 0.0223; nonpatent prior art p = 0.0282). Also report area-specific significance (software p = 0.0024; mechanical p = 0.0004; industry: computer and pharmaceutical p < 0.0001). Note limitations: small sample (106 observations), many correlated variables, and non-mutually-exclusive technology/industry assignments increase interactions—interpret coefficients cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification decision rule for self-citations (manual verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational rule used to label a forward citation as a self-citation: (a) owners of the main patent and the forward citation are the same; or (b) owners differ but inventors are the same and there are no co-inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors manually examined front pages of 3419 forward-citing patents to apply this rule. Economists sometimes use a blunter, automatable test (assignee-equality), which misses nuance. Acknowledge potential misidentification when ownership has changed or multiple inventors exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about correlated patent characteristics and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent metrics are highly correlated (e.g., number of claims, prior art types, number of applications, forward citations) because applicants anticipating value/difficulty tend to draft differently and cite more art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of common-cause and reverse causation: applicant behavior (more claims, continuations, citations) both reflects and creates perceived value and later citation patterns. Correlations complicate multivariate analysis; small sample sizes further limit statistical power. Use robustness checks and be explicit about causal limitations.
